intro/before: Chapter eleven said what a ConvNet is. This chapter is about making one work, on a real problem, with a real budget.
intro/q1: First: you never have enough labeled images. How do you stretch the ones you have?
intro/q2: Second, how do you reuse a network that someone else trained on a million images?
intro/q3: Third, which convolutions should you stack, and how are they computed fast?
intro/q4: And fourth, what hardware and software does it all run on?
intro/go: Let us start with the data.
augment/few: A ConvNet has millions of parameters, so it can simply memorize a few thousand images.
augment/trick: A cheap defense: change the training images in ways that keep their labels. A flipped cat is still a cat.
augment/loop: So the training loop gets one extra step: load an image and its label, transform the image at random, then compute the loss.
augment/every: Every epoch the network sees a new version, and the only constant, the cat, is what it has to learn.
augment/flip: First, horizontal flips: with probability one half, reverse the order of the columns.
augment/updown: Vertical flips are usually a bad idea, since the world has an up and a down.
augment/crop: Second, random crops and scales. Res net picks a length L between two fifty six and four eighty. It resizes the image so its shorter side is L.
augment/patch: Then it cuts out a random two twenty four by two twenty four patch, so the object lands at a new size, in a new place, every time.
augment/test: At test time there is no randomness. Instead, average the predictions over a fixed set of crops:
augment/ten: the four corners and the center, plus their mirror images, ten crops in all.
color/jitter: Third, color jitter. The simplest version scales the contrast at random.
color/alex: Alex net was more careful. It shifted colors along the directions in which they vary across the dataset.
color/cloud: Picture every training pixel as a dot in three dimensions, with red, green and blue as the axes.
color/eig: The covariance matrix of these dots has eigenvectors: the natural axes of the cloud. Each eigenvalue, lambda, is the spread along its axis.
color/bright: The first axis is almost equal parts red, green and blue: brightness. The others trade colors against each other.
color/shift: For each image, draw three small random amounts, alpha, with a spread of zero point one, and add one color offset to every pixel.
color/light: It looks like the same scene under slightly different light: a change that should never alter the label.
color/creative: Beyond that, get creative: rotations, stretching, shearing. Anything that changes the pixels but not the label.
color/six: What makes sense depends on the data: rotate a six by a hundred and eighty degrees, and it becomes a nine.
noise/theme: Augmentation is one case of a pattern that runs through this whole course.
noise/rule: During training, add random noise. At test time, average the noise away.
noise/drop: Dropout zeroes random activations in training. At test time, it uses their expected value. DropConnect does the same to weights.
noise/bn: Batch normalization uses noisy mini-batch statistics in training, and fixed averages at test time.
noise/ens: An ensemble averages networks that started from different random weights.
noise/aug: And augmentation puts the noise in the input, while test-time crops average it out.
noise/eq: Written as an equation: the probability of class y given X is about the average, over M fixed views, of each view's answer.
noise/cost: That smooths out the luck of any single crop. The price: M forward passes per image.
transfer/scratch: The other half of making the most of your data is not starting from scratch.
transfer/myth: You do not need a huge dataset to use ConvNets. Features learned on ImageNet, one point two million images in a thousand classes, help with almost any visual task.
transfer/two: So people download a network trained on ImageNet, and use it in one of two ways.
transfer/extract: One: as a fixed feature extractor. Remove the last layer, the thousand ImageNet scores.
transfer/codes: What remains turns each image into four thousand and ninety six numbers, after a ray-loo: its CNN codes. Then train a linear classifier on them.
transfer/strong: This simple recipe is remarkably strong. One paper called it an astounding baseline.
transfer/finetune: Two: fine-tuning. Replace the classifier, and keep training the pretrained weights on your own data.
transfer/freeze: You can freeze the early layers, which hold generic edge and color detectors, and fine-tune only the top.
transfer/specific: The top layers are more specific. ImageNet has many dog breeds, so much of the top is busy telling dogs apart.
transfer/zoo: Training on ImageNet took weeks, so people share their trained weights, like caff-ay's Model Zoo.
strategy/two: Which strategy, when? It depends on how much data you have, and how similar it is to ImageNet.
strategy/c1: Little data, similar images: fine-tuning would overfit, but the top features fit. Train a linear classifier on the CNN codes.
strategy/c2: Lots of data, similar images: fine-tune the top few layers, or all of them.
strategy/c3: Little data, very different images, like X-rays: the hard case. Try linear classifiers on earlier, more generic layers.
strategy/c4: Lots of data, very different images: fine-tune a large part of the network. Pretrained weights still beat random ones as a start.
strategy/noisy: When you fine-tune, the pretrained weights are already good, while a fresh head sends back large, noisy gradients.
strategy/rates: So the head gets the full learning rate, eta. The top layers get a tenth, the middle a hundredth, and frozen layers zero.
strategy/caffe: In caff-ay, that is one multiplier per layer, and zero freezes it.
strategy/norm: Transfer learning is the norm. Object detectors and captioning systems start from ImageNet ConvNets too.
strategy/advice: With fewer than a million images, find a big, similar dataset, train or download a ConvNet on it, and transfer.
stack/recall: Chapter eleven favored stacks of small three by three filters for their fewer weights. The same holds for compute.
stack/setup: Take an H by H by C volume, and layers of C filters that keep it H by H by C.
stack/cost: Each output costs one multiply-add per filter weight, and each layer has H times H times C outputs.
stack/seven: One seven by seven layer: forty nine C weights per output, so forty nine, H squared, C squared.
stack/three: Three three by three layers see the same seven by seven patch, for three times nine: twenty seven, H squared, C squared.
stack/good: Nearly half the compute, and three ray-loos instead of one. The lecture called that good, in capital letters.
stack/why: Why stop there? A one by one convolution only mixes the channels at each pixel: a cheap way to change depth.
stack/squeeze: The bottleneck squeezes the channels down to half with a one by one layer,
stack/middle: does the three by three work at half depth, for a quarter of the cost,
stack/expand: and expands back with another one by one: three and a quarter C squared, instead of nine.
stack/factor: Even a three by three splits into a one by three and a three by one: six C squared instead of nine. For N by N, two N instead of N squared.
stack/bars: Line the five designs up: fewer parameters, less compute, more nonlinearity, whatever C and H are.
im2col/how: So how does a computer compute a convolution fast?
im2col/blas: Matrix multiplication is tuned to the last instruction on every platform: blass on C P Us, coo blass on G P Us.
im2col/idea: So the common trick, im to coal, rearranges a convolution into one big matrix multiply.
im2col/patch: Take a five by five input X and a three by three window. At each of its nine positions, take the patch,
im2col/col: read it row by row, and stand it up as a column of X col.
im2col/repeat: The same inputs land in several columns: the middle pixel is in all nine.
im2col/wrow: Then stretch each filter into a row: with two filters, W row is two by nine.
im2col/mm: One matrix product does it all: row k times column m is filter k dotted with patch m, one output.
im2col/reshape: And a reshape turns each row of the result into a three by three activation map.
im2col/cost: The price is memory: for Alex net's first layer, X col is seven times bigger than the image. Caff-ay does exactly this.
fast/theorem: A second approach: the convolution theorem.
fast/waves: The Fourier transform rewrites a signal as a sum of waves, and convolution becomes an elementwise product of transforms.
fast/steps: Transform the image, transform the flipped filter, multiply, and transform back.
fast/nlogn: The fast Fourier transform does n numbers in about n log n steps, not n squared. Big wins for big filters, small ones for three by three.
fast/strassen: The third approach is clever algebra: trade multiplications for cheaper additions, as Strassen did for matrix products.
fast/lavin: In twenty fifteen, Lavin and Gray did that for three by three convolutions, with Win-oh-grad's algorithms.
fast/direct: The smallest case: two outputs of a three-tap filter g, over four inputs d. Done directly, that is six multiplications.
fast/G: The fast way first mixes the filter into four numbers, G: once per filter, then reused at every position.
fast/m: Then four products, each a sum or difference of inputs, times one G.
fast/y: Add and subtract them: the same two outputs, from four multiplications instead of six.
fast/tile: In two dimensions, a two by two tile takes sixteen instead of thirty six. coo D N N added it in twenty sixteen.
fast/sum: To sum up: im to coal is easy but memory hungry. The F F T suits large filters, and Win-oh-grad the small ones.
hardware/cpu: All this runs on hardware. A C P U has a few fast cores, good at doing one thing after another.
hardware/gpu: A G P U has thousands of slower cores. They do one simple operation on lots of data at once: exactly what convolutions are.
hardware/nvidia: En-vidia leads, thanks to coo-da and its libraries, coo blass and coo D N N, which the frameworks call for you.
hardware/copy: Watch for bottlenecks. Moving data to the G P U is slow. So prepare the next batch on the C P U, in a separate thread.
hardware/disk: Disks choke on millions of small files: store the images in one big file, and stream it from an S S D.
hardware/mem: And memory is tight: twelve gigabytes on the biggest G P U of early twenty sixteen.
hardware/data: Several G P Us can share the work. In data parallelism, each holds the whole model, and takes a slice of the batch.
hardware/model: In model parallelism, the model itself is split. Krizhevsky split his fully connected layers this way.
hardware/sync: Synchronous training waits for everyone, averages the gradients, and updates: exactly one big batch, just faster.
hardware/async: Asynchronous training updates a shared copy whenever a worker finishes: no waiting, but slightly stale weights.
precision/bits: One more hardware question: how many bits per number?
precision/f64: NumPy uses sixty four bit doubles by default.
precision/f32: ConvNets train in thirty two bit single precision: half the memory, and accurate enough.
precision/f16: The lecture predicted sixteen bits would become standard. Research went lower still, even to one bit.
precision/danger: The danger is small numbers getting rounded away. Just below one, float sixteen values are about five ten-thousandths apart.
precision/stuck: So a step of one ten-thousandth, on a weight of one, rounds straight back to one. Every single time.
precision/sr: The fix is stochastic rounding: round up at random. The chance of up is how far the value is past the lower neighbor.
precision/avg: Each rounding is off, but on average it is exactly right. So the weight tracks the truth.
precision/gupta: With it, Gupta and colleagues trained networks in sixteen bit fixed point.
software/nobody: Nobody writes a serious ConvNet in raw NumPy. In twenty sixteen, four frameworks led: caff-ay, Torch, thee-ah-no and tensor flow.
software/jobs: All of them solve the same two problems: run fast on G P Us, and compute the gradients for you.
software/graph: A network is a computational graph. Backprop is the chain rule, run backward through it.
software/auto: So a framework that knows the graph does backprop for you: you write only the forward pass.
software/sym: In thee-ah-no, you first build the graph from symbolic variables that hold no data yet.
software/compile: Then you ask for the gradients, symbolically, and compile it all into a function.
software/run: Only then do you run it, on real arrays.
software/tf: Tensor flow, from Google, is the same plan with new names: placeholders, Variables, and a Session. Both shine for unusual recurrent nets.
software/caffe: Caff-ay, from Berkeley, describes ConvNets in text files, so you can fine-tune from its Model Zoo without writing code.
software/torch: Torch has NumPy-like arrays and short, readable layers, so new layers are easy. But it is in loo-ah.
software/later: It all moved fast. Pie torch arrived in twenty seventeen, building the graph as the code runs, and soon became the default for research.
outro/r1: That is ConvNets in practice. Stretch your data with label-keeping noise, and average fixed views at test time.
outro/r2: Start from an ImageNet model, and fine-tune more of it as your data grows and differs.
outro/r3: Stack small filters and bottlenecks: fewer parameters, less compute, more nonlinearity.
outro/r4: Underneath, convolutions become matrix multiplies, F F Ts or Win-oh-grad tricks, on G P Us, in fewer and fewer bits.
outro/r5: And let a framework derive the gradients.
outro/next: Next, open the interactive chapter. Augment real see-far ten images, pick a transfer strategy, and try im to coal yourself.
